title: Is Depression a Spiritual Failure?
excerpt: Many believers in the dark have been told to pray more and trust more. Elijah, the psalmists, Job and Paul went to the bottom and were not told it was their fault, and Scripture treats a person as dust and breath together, so prayer and a doctor were never rivals.
body:
A woman has asked her small group to pray for her for most of a year, and last week one of them told her, with real affection, that the joy of the Lord is her strength. A man who teaches a Sunday class takes a pill every morning and has never told anyone at church, because he once heard a sermon that called such things a crutch for people who will not trust God. A student was advised that sadness which won't lift usually means sin which hasn't been confessed, and he has spent months searching his memory for the sin.

The skeptic has seen this before and has a name for it. A religion promises peace, he says, and when the peace doesn't come it blames the customer.

This essay can't tell any reader what is wrong, and it is not medical advice. It should say first where help is. The site keeps a page for the person who feels [empty and doesn't know why](/help/empty), and [Find Help](/help) has the telephone lines and the other pages. Two things from that page belong at the top of this one. None of this means you're weak or that your faith has failed. And of the darkness itself the page says this: It can change. If it has turned into thoughts of ending your life, call or text 988 now.

## The Charge

The idea that depression is a spiritual failure is usually put more gently than that. It comes as advice: pray more, trust more, spend more time in the word, count what you have been given. The people who give it are seldom cruel. Most of them are trying to help with the only tools they were handed, and their case deserves to be stated properly before it is answered.

Scripture does command joy. "Rejoice in the Lord always" (Philippians 4:4) is an order, and so is "do not be anxious about anything" (Philippians 4:6). Scripture also knows a misery that comes from sin. David wrote of a season of hidden guilt, "when I kept silent, my bones wasted away through my groaning all day long" (Psalm 32:3), and the cure in that psalm was confession. Those who press the spiritual explanation fear two things, and neither is foolish. They fear that a real sin will be renamed a symptom and never repented of, and they fear a church that sends its wounded to the pharmacy and stops believing that Christ has anything to say to a darkened mind.

Some of that has to be granted. Guilt can make a person ill, and where guilt is the trouble, forgiveness helps as nothing else will. Prayer and Scripture are real helps and no one should be talked out of them. Unbelief exists.

But the charge goes further than that. It says that a believer who is cast down and stays down has failed at believing. That claim can be tested against the Bible's own people, and it does not survive them.

## What Scripture Shows

Start with Elijah. He had just stood alone against the prophets of Baal and seen fire fall. One threat from the queen and he ran a day into the desert, sat under a tree, "and he asked that he might die" (1 Kings 19:4). If ever a man deserved the lecture about trusting more, it was the one who had so lately watched the fire come down. No lecture is given. An angel touches him and says, "Arise and eat" (1 Kings 19:5). He eats, and sleeps again. The angel comes a second time with the same food and a reason, which is that the road ahead is too much for him (1 Kings 19:7). God's first response to a prophet who had asked to die was a meal and a night's sleep, and then another meal. The conversation came weeks later, and when it did, God answered his "I only am left" by giving him a companion and telling him of seven thousand others.

The psalms go further, because they are prayers the whole people were given to sing. "My tears have been my food day and night," says one (Psalm 42:3). The writer argues with himself, "Why are you cast down, O my soul?" and he tells himself to hope, but he puts the praise in the future tense: "I shall again praise him" (Psalm 42:5). He isn't praising yet. Psalm 88 never gets even that far. It begins by crying to God day and night and it ends, "You have caused my beloved and my friend to shun me; my companions have become darkness" (Psalm 88:18). There is no turn toward hope in it at all. Someone wrote that prayer, Israel kept it, and it is Scripture.

Job, when the worst had happened, "opened his mouth and cursed the day of his birth" (Job 3:1). His friends then supplied the theory this essay is about. "Who that was innocent ever perished?" one of them asked (Job 4:7). If Job was suffering like this, there was a cause in Job, and he should find it and repent. They argued it with great skill for most of the book. At the end God spoke to them directly: "you have not spoken of me what is right, as my servant Job has" (Job 42:7). The man who had cursed his birthday was the one who had spoken rightly. The men with the explanation had not.

Then there is Paul, who can hardly be accused of weak faith. He wrote to Corinth about what happened to him in Asia: "we were so utterly burdened beyond our strength that we despaired of life itself" (2 Corinthians 1:8). Later in the same letter he says that he arrived in Macedonia with "fighting without and fear within," and that God "comforted us by the coming of Titus" (2 Corinthians 7:5-6). The comfort of God, for an apostle, came through a friend walking in the door.

And there is the Lord himself, in the garden on the last night: "My soul is very sorrowful, even to death" (Mark 14:34).

Scripture gives these people more than permission to speak. It also shows what hope looked like for them, and it was seldom a feeling. The poet of Lamentations says, "my soul is bereft of peace; I have forgotten what happiness is" (Lamentations 3:17). A few lines on he writes, "But this I call to mind, and therefore I have hope: The steadfast love of the Lord never ceases" (Lamentations 3:21-22). Nothing in his circumstances has changed between the two sentences, and he does not claim to feel better. He remembers something. In the Bible hope is often an act of memory carried out by someone who feels nothing yet, and that is very different from being told to cheer up.

Care is needed here. None of these passages is a medical report, and it would be a mistake to read a modern diagnosis back into Elijah or the psalmist. Scripture doesn't use our clinical words. What it shows is narrower and enough: the most faithful people in the book went to the bottom, said so out loud, and were not told that their darkness was their fault.

## Dust and Breath

The Bible's account of what a human being is explains why. "The Lord God formed the man of dust from the ground and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life, and the man became a living creature" (Genesis 2:7). A person is a single creature made of both, and what happens to the body happens to the whole person. "He knows our frame; he remembers that we are dust" (Psalm 103:14). It is why the angel brought Elijah bread and why Paul told Timothy to take "a little wine for the sake of your stomach and your frequent ailments" (1 Timothy 5:23). One of Paul's closest companions he called "the beloved physician" (Colossians 4:14).

The church's best pastors have known this for a long time. In the 1870s Charles Spurgeon, the best-known preacher in Victorian London, gave his ministry students a lecture on their own low spirits. Almost his first words were these: "Fits of depression come over the most of us." He described a kind that arrives with no reason attached. "Causeless depression is not to be reasoned with," he said, and he compared fighting it to fighting mist. He pointed to Luther, whose life "might suffice to give a thousand instances, and he was by no means of the weaker sort." And he sent his students outdoors. A stiff walk in the wind, he told them, "would not give grace to the soul, but it would yield oxygen to the body, which is next best."

The site's page on emptiness makes the same point in today's terms. It says that depression "is a real medical condition, it's common, and it's treatable," and it notes that some illnesses and medicines produce the same flatness, which is one reason a doctor is the right person to see. It also carries these words, which matter for the man with the pill bottle: Depression is treatable, counseling helps many people, and if a doctor recommends medication, taking it is not a failure of faith.

The older spiritual writers drew a distinction that is still useful. The same page tells of John of the Cross, a friar in Spain in the 1500s, who described a season when prayer goes dry because God is teaching someone to want him and not the feeling of him. He called it the dark night. That is a real experience and it is not an illness. But the friar also taught that not every dryness is that night, and the page draws the conclusion for a reader today: "A dark night is never a reason to skip the doctor." A pastor who can't tell the two apart should say so, and should send for help with the part he can't judge.

## Three Answers

Christians have given three answers to the question in the title, and the first two are each half of something.

The first is the one already described: the darkness is spiritual, and the remedy is repentance and faith. It is right that a human being has a soul, that guilt and unbelief are real, and that Christ speaks to the mind. It is wrong when it treats the body as if it were not there.

The second answer is the opposite, and it is common now inside the church as well as outside it. Depression is chemistry, the remedy is medical, and faith has nothing to do with it either way. This is kinder than the first, and it is right that the body is involved. But it also leaves out half the creature. A person in the dark is asking questions that no prescription addresses: whether her life means anything, whether God has left, whether she is forgiven. A church that answers every such question with a referral has stopped doing its own work. The same page on this site says of the medical, the psychological and the spiritual accounts that "taken alone, each leaves out the rest of you."

The third answer holds the two together. A believer in the dark may need a doctor, and a counselor, and the Lord's Table, and a friend who brings dinner on Thursday, and none of these competes with the others. Among Christians who hold this there is still an honest disagreement about proportion. Some trust pastoral care from Scripture most and are wary of counsel that rests on assumptions about human beings the Bible doesn't share. Others see in medicine and counseling the ordinary kindness of God, the same kindness that gives bread, and think the church has been slow to receive it. Each of them fears something that has really happened. What neither of them may do is set prayer against the doctor. Scripture never does.

## What Prayer Is For

Where does that leave the advice to pray more? Prayer is not the problem. The use of prayer as a measuring stick is.

When prayer is prescribed as the cure for low spirits, the person's recovery becomes a grade on her praying. If she is still in the dark in a month, she has been told in effect that she prayed badly. The psalms cut against that. Psalm 88 is a prayer, and nothing gets better in it. It is given to the church as something a believer may say to God when nothing has improved, and saying it is itself faith. Paul adds a promise for the person who can't manage even that: "we do not know what to pray for as we ought, but the Spirit himself intercedes for us with groanings too deep for words" (Romans 8:26). The essay here on [whether prayer changes anything](/writing/does-prayer-change-anything) takes the larger question. On this narrower one the answer is plain. Prayer is for bringing the darkness to God. It was never meant to prove that someone doesn't have any.

## What We Did

The church should have been the easiest place on earth to admit to not being all right. We made it one of the hardest.

We quoted the joy of the Lord at people who could not find it, and forgot where the sentence comes from. Nehemiah said it to a crowd that was weeping, and what he told them to do was go home, eat well, and "send portions to anyone who has nothing ready" (Nehemiah 8:10). He was sending them to dinner and to their neighbors. He wasn't giving them a rebuke. We built services in which only victories were reported from the front, so that everyone in the room assumed he was the only one losing. We let people believe that the pill in the cabinet was a secret to be kept from the family of God. Proverbs had already told us what our cheerfulness was worth: "Whoever sings songs to a heavy heart is like one who takes off a garment on a cold day" (Proverbs 25:20).

We have failed the other way as well. Telling a person to see a professional can be love, and it can also be a way of getting a suffering person out of the room. Job's friends did one thing well. Before they opened their mouths they kept him company in silence for a week, "and no one spoke a word to him, for they saw that his suffering was very great" (Job 2:13). Much of the harm we have done began when we stopped sitting there and started explaining.

## If It Is You

Nothing in this essay knows what any reader is carrying, and it would be wrong to guess. A few things can be said to anyone.

What you feel is not a ruling on your faith. Elijah, the psalmists, Job and Paul were not failing. The practical steps belong to people who can know you: a doctor, a counselor, a pastor, one friend who is told the truth. The page for the person who [feels empty](/help/empty) sets out small ones, and it is worth reading slowly. You don't have to be suicidal to call or text 988; it's there for anyone in emotional distress. [Find Help](/help) has the rest. If the trouble is mostly that God seems absent, the essay on [why God feels so far away](/writing/why-does-god-feel-far-away) is about that.

Isaiah said of the servant God would send, "a bruised reed he will not break, and a faintly burning wick he will not quench" (Isaiah 42:3). Christians believe that servant came. The Gospels do not show him telling a crushed person to try harder.

The woman whose friends told her about the joy of the Lord may still be waiting for it. Psalm 42 lets her say that she will praise again without pretending that she can today. Psalm 88 lets her say less than that. And under the tree in the desert the first words God sent to the man who had asked to die were about food. Elijah would be questioned later, and when the question came his answer was the same complaint he had started with. God did not call it a failure of faith. He gave him someone to travel with and sent him back down the mountain.

*"The Lord is near to the brokenhearted and saves the crushed in spirit."* (Psalm 34:18)

*"A bruised reed he will not break, and a faintly burning wick he will not quench."* (Isaiah 42:3)
